clue.text: Former boss of North Korea gang lands

indicators.note: to land something is to catch and hold it, so the run of words holds the solution inside

parts.note: found across the end of Korea and the start of gang

explanation.surface: A one-time North Korean crime boss whose gang has arrived somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The North Korea picture hides the real former boss: Ronald Reagan, sitting in koREA GANg.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was once US President, the head of the American government, so he is a past boss.

clue.text: From a distance, right, turn volume up … see?

parts.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right

indicators.note: to turn something round is to face it the other way
in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

parts.note: a tome is a large book or volume
Ely is a cathedral city, a bishop's see

explanation.surface: Instructions for a remote control: sit back, turn the volume up and look.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; Ely, a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, is the crossword favourite. R plus EMOT plus ELY gives REMOTELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something remotely means acting at a distance rather than in person, so the adverb phrase matches.

clue.text: Novel with a title encompassing plot

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: encompassing means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: Dame is a title given to a woman
a plot of garden is a bed

explanation.surface: A novel with a title that wraps up the whole plot.
explanation.walkthrough: A DAME surrounds BED to give ADAM BEDE, George Eliot's first novel. 'Plot' looks like a story's plot but means a garden bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Bede is an 1859 novel by George Eliot, named for its carpenter hero.

clue.text: In a state of frenzy, flipping curry runs out!

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it back to front
runs out means the cricket abbreviation for runs leaves the word

parts.note: a korma is a mild curry
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone goes into a frenzy, swearing, because the curry has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word but turns KORMA round to AMROK; the R then goes, leaving AMOK.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to behave wildly and out of control, which is a frenzied state.

clue.text: Shelled shellfish crossing a hundred pound barrier

indicators.note: crossing here means stretched across, so the outer letters span the inserted ones
with its shell removed, the word loses its outside letters

parts.note: a lobster is a shellfish
taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A seafood stall with a barrier priced at a hundred pounds, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: LOBSTER without its outer letters is OBSTE, which goes round A C L to make OBSTACLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle is anything that blocks the way, the same job a barrier does.

clue.text: Bishop questioning extortionist, a fishy character

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to question is to ask
a loan shark or swindler is called a shark

explanation.surface: A bishop interrogating a racketeer, a dubious type himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fishy character' suggests someone shady, but here it is literally a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The basking shark is a huge plankton-eating fish, so it is a creature of the sea, literally fishy.

clue.text: Muppet from the south abandoning M1 journey

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading from the south means starting at the bottom and going up
to abandon something is to leave it behind, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: Kermit the Frog is the best-known Muppet
M and 1 read as M and I, the letters to take out

explanation.surface: A Muppet heading up from the south avoids the M1, England's main north-south motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: KERMIT read upwards is TIMREK; the M and I (the 1 of M1 read as a letter) come out, leaving TREK.
explanation.definitionFit: A trek is a long, arduous journey, usually on foot.

clue.text: Exhausted county tennis champ who's a bit robotic?

indicators.note: something exhausted has been emptied out, so only the shell of the word is kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of county
Bjorn Borg won Wimbledon five times running

explanation.surface: A worn-out county tennis champion whose play has become mechanical.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by description: a being that is partly machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyborg is part human and part machine, so it is partly a robot.

clue.text: Former partner desolate, with yen to run free

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: the letter for yen runs off, leaving the word

parts.note: desolate means empty
Y is the abbreviation for yen, the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: A desolate ex longs to run away and be free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like longing but is the Japanese currency; its Y leaves EMPTY.
explanation.definitionFit: To be exempt is to be freed from an obligation that applies to others.

clue.text: Field cut outside each day

indicators.note: outside means going round, so one word surrounds the rest

parts.note: to mow is to cut grass
EA is the abbreviation for each
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A field of grass that is cut every day.
explanation.definitionFit: A meadow is a field of grass, often grown for hay.

clue.text: Gather sister regularly dropped the pace when walking laps

indicators.note: to lap is to wrap round, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: an amble is a slow, easy walking pace

indicators.note: dropping regularly means every other letter goes, keeping alternate ones

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of sister

explanation.surface: Collecting a sister whose walking pace slowed as she did laps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laps' looks like circuits of a track, but here it means wraps around.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to come together or to bring things together, which is what gathering means.

clue.text: Golf tournament on Kent course for which a slice will do the trick?

definitions.text: for which a slice will do the trick?

parts.note: the Open is the oldest major golf championship
Royal St George's at Sandwich in Kent hosts the Open

explanation.surface: A golfer at the Open at Sandwich, where a sliced shot might win it.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf a slice is a bad curving shot; in the kitchen it is the single piece of bread this dish needs. Sandwich is a town in Kent with a famous golf links.
explanation.definitionFit: An open sandwich uses one slice of bread with the filling on top, so one slice is enough.

clue.text: Returned neighbour's instrument

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: to neighbour is to border on, or abut

explanation.surface: Giving back the neighbour's borrowed musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neighbour' is a verb here, and the 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuba is a large, low-pitched brass instrument.

clue.text: Country home to the east of Belgian city

indicators.note: in an across answer, to the east means written to the right, so this piece follows

parts.note: Spa is a Belgian town that gave its name to spas
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A country home east of a Belgian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a European country on the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Wham's first hip hop cover

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of Wham
rap is hip hop music

explanation.surface: Wham!, the 1980s pop duo, recording a hip hop cover version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests a cover version of a song but is simply the noun or verb wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrap is something you cover with, and to wrap is to cover.

clue.text: Around 1st of January, wade across narrow inlet

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one word goes round the letter

parts.note: to ford a river is to wade across it

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of January

explanation.surface: Wading across a narrow sea inlet around the start of January, a chilly prospect.
explanation.definitionFit: A fjord is a long, narrow inlet of sea between steep cliffs, as in Norway.

clue.text: Wooded country with rolling dale

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with

indicators.note: rolling things tumble over, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Describes English countryside: woods and rolling valleys.
explanation.walkthrough: The Weald is the once-forested area of Kent and Sussex in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The word weald originally meant woodland or forest, so it names wooded country.

clue.text: Left angry deejay playing Queen

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: playing about with letters moves them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A furious DJ walked out while a Queen song was playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' suggests the rock band a DJ might play, but it is a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed Queen of England in 1553 and reigned for nine days.

clue.text: Shockingly, Sun hires escorts

indicators.note: shockingly means badly or in disarray, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid scandal: the Sun newspaper hires escorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Escorts' looks like a noun in a headline but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher someone in is to show or escort them inside.

clue.text: Simon had woven carpet

indicators.note: woven threads are interlaced into a new pattern, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Simon had a carpet woven for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' is a verb here: in British usage, to carpet someone is to reprimand them.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to call them in for a telling-off, which is to admonish them.

clue.text: Floundering badly, Theresa is tested by the police

indicators.note: floundering means struggling clumsily, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Theresa, staggering badly, is stopped and tested by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' looks like part of the anagram signal but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Being breathalysed means being given a breath test by police to check for alcohol.

clue.text: Israeli spies not unhappy upsetting their US colleagues; it's a complex picture

indicators.note: not means without, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: Mossad is Israel's intelligence agency
unhappy means sad

indicators.note: to upset is to turn over, so in a down entry the word is read upwards

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Israeli spies, quite cheerful about upsetting their American counterparts; the whole affair is complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not unhappy' reads as pleased, but it tells you to remove SAD from MOSSAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosaic is a picture made of many small pieces, so it is an intricate image.

clue.text: Reflective article in newspaper?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a glass object that reflects
second meaning: a British daily tabloid

explanation.surface: A thoughtful opinion piece printed in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflective article' sounds like a thoughtful essay but is a looking-glass; the Daily Mirror is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror is a reflecting object, and the Mirror is a well-known UK newspaper title.

clue.text: Overlook Holmfirth occasionally

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of Holmfirth

explanation.surface: Holmfirth, a small Yorkshire town, is something people sometimes overlook.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit something is to leave it out, the same as to overlook it.

clue.text: After date, actress Sophia undressed to make love

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the next piece follows this one
undressed means stripped of clothes, so the outer letters come off

parts.note: AD, anno domini, is the label on a date
Sophia Loren is the Italian film star

explanation.surface: After a date, a film star takes her clothes off to make love.
explanation.walkthrough: Undressing a name strips its first and last letters, as if removing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love them deeply.

clue.text: Ban doctor beginning to operate

parts.note: a vet is an animal doctor

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of operate

explanation.surface: A doctor is banned from starting to operate.
explanation.definitionFit: A veto is an official refusal or prohibition, which is a ban.

clue.text: Possible home for Asian global investment banks

indicators.note: to bank something is to deposit and hold it, so the phrase keeps the solution inside

parts.note: found across the end of global and the start of investment

explanation.surface: Somewhere an Asian global investment bank might be based.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like the financial institutions but is a verb meaning holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Bali is an Indonesian island, so it could be where an Asian person lives.

clue.text: A way to dismiss British Member of Parliament

definitions.note: a verb defined by a noun phrase: bowling is one way to get a batsman out

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a group of owls is called a parliament

explanation.surface: A way to get rid of a British MP.
explanation.walkthrough: Member of Parliament looks like an MP but is a bird, as a group of owls is a parliament. In cricket, a batsman can be dismissed by being bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl a batsman out is a standard method of dismissal in cricket.

clue.text: Hire vehicles without charge, teacher travelling back first class

parts.note: A1 means first class, read as AI

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one word goes round the other
travelling back means going the opposite way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: pupils call a male teacher sir
a tax is a charge

explanation.surface: Hiring vehicles free of charge, with a teacher travelling home first class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without charge' reads as free, but without here means outside, an old sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Air taxis are small planes chartered for short trips, so they are aircraft you hire.

clue.text: Setter — a social elitist — knocked over potted plant

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up the other way round

parts.note: the setter refers to himself as I
taken as written
a snob looks down on those of lower social standing

explanation.surface: The setter, a snob, knocks over a potted plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonsai is a miniature tree grown in a pot.

clue.text: Drive with sea view my delightful husband put in

parts.note: cor! is a British exclamation like my!

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so a letter goes into the word

parts.note: nice means pleasant or delightful
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A wife praising a husband who has driven her along a scenic coast road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation, the British cor! of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a road cut along a coastal cliff, giving views of the sea.

clue.text: Consuming large beer by hotel block, maybe under the table?

indicators.note: consuming means taking in, so one word swallows the other

parts.note: a pint is a glass of beer
L is the abbreviation for large
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Drinking a large beer at a hotel until ending up under the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under the table' suggests drunk, but here it is the base a table might stand on.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth is a heavy base block placed under a column, statue or piece of furniture.
